criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and municipal water supply and sanitation (WSS) service coverage, tariff affordability, access to water social tariff programs, and connection fee burdens in Brazil.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism clarification: under the plain wording, it analyzes WSS tariff regulation, social assistance targeting, and state-owned/capital utility pricing structures; under the narrow rule-type reading, it directly evaluates tariff and cost-recovery schedules, social tariff discounts (comparing affordability with vs. without social tariffs), eligibility/take-up gaps in social tariff programs relative to CADÚnico low-income eligibility, and upfront utility connection fee rules governing household connection access.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains a quantitative empirical case study of Brazil across 4,052 municipalities served by state-owned WSS utilities (plus state capitals), combining secondary administrative and survey data from SNIS (2021/2022), IBGE Census 2022, PNADC 2023, CADÚnico (September 2023), and October 2023 utility tariff and connection fee schedules.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports outcomes directly relevant to WSS coverage rates (SNIS IN055 and IN056), conventional and poorer-household WSS affordability ratios (with and without social tariffs), percentage of eligible low-income households accessing social tariffs, and connection fee burden as a share of monthly household income.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (4,052 Brazilian municipalities and state-level population/household income groups within state-owned and capital WSS utility areas), rule-type exposures (tariff structures, social tariff discounts/eligibility rules, and initial WSS connection fees), outcomes (coverage, affordability ratios, social tariff take-up, connection fee burden), and cross-sectional quantitative design are all clearly identifiable. Note that whether effect estimates can be pooled quantitatively is a Criterion 6 synthesis-eligibility gate rather than a systematic-review inclusion gate.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: This paper proposes a broader affordability analysis framework, considering six main dimensions, coverage rates, conventional affordability ratio, poverty condition of the community, affordability ratio for poorer households, access to water social programs, and connection fee burden.

Despite the different rules the state’s WSS companies applied to their social tariff programs, the affordability ratio for poorer households considered the income as 1/2 minimum wage and the WSS tariff with and without discount applied by each utility for social tariff.

This paper compared the number of urban low-income families in each state (earning ½ minimum wage or less in September 2023, from CADÚnico) with the number of households accessing social tariffs users, data from SNIS.

Therefore, the sample encompasses all the cities where those state-owned companies provide water supply and/or sanitation services, reaching 4052 municipalities, representing 72.8% of Brazilian cities, 78.9% of the total population for water supply services, and 60.1% of wastewater collection and/or treatment
Figure 9 displays the percentage of cities in Brazil that would spend more than 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, and 100% of their monthly income on WSS connection fees, payable to utilities.

raw_response.exposure: Utility WSS tariff schedules, social tariff discounts and eligibility/access rules, and upfront water and wastewater connection fee schedules across Brazilian state-owned and state-capital WSS providers.
raw_response.outcome: Water supply and sanitation coverage rates (SNIS IN055, IN056), household WSS affordability ratios (conventional and poorer-household ratios with vs. without social tariffs), social tariff access (%) among eligible low-income families, and connection fee burden (% of monthly household income).
raw_response.population_and_sample: Households and populations across 4,052 Brazilian municipalities (72.8% of Brazilian cities) served by state-owned WSS companies and state-capital utilities, aggregated at municipal and state levels across average-wage and low-income (<= 1/2 minimum wage in CADÚnico and 60% of average state wage) household groups.
raw_response.rationale: The study satisfies all systematic-review inclusion criteria (c1-c6). Alongside proposing an analytical framework, Section 3 conducts an empirical cross-sectional quantitative analysis of 4,052 Brazilian municipalities using SNIS, IBGE Census/PNADC, CADÚnico, and utility tariff schedules. It directly examines rule-type mechanisms under Criterion 2 (tariff structures, social tariff discounts and eligibility/take-up gaps, and initial connection fee schedules) and reports household/municipal WSS coverage, affordability ratios with and without social tariffs, social tariff access rates among eligible poor families, and connection fee burdens.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional quantitative empirical analysis (multi-utility municipal/state secondary administrative, survey, and tariff-schedule study)
